strengths: The paper provides a well-organized and fairly convincing set of motivating experiments (Section 2) across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and BridgeDataV2/SimplerEnv that empirically demonstrate the 'vision shortcut' phenomenon, including a clean information-theoretic framing (conditional mutual information / entropy bound) that gives conceptual grounding for the proposed fix.

The core idea of instantiating a Bayesian decomposition via a dual-branch (prior/posterior) architecture sharing weights through causal-masking control of Latent Action Queries is an elegant and computationally cheap mechanism (no extra inference-time cost) that is reasonably well motivated by the PMI/LLR derivation in Appendix A.

Empirical results (Table 1, Table 2) show consistent improvements over the same-framework baseline (QwenGR00T) on both SimplerEnv (55.2% -> 66.5%) and RoboCasa (47.8% -> 50.4%), and the ablation (Table 3) isolates the contribution of Latent Action Queries alone versus the full dual-branch LLR objective, showing both contribute positively.

The qualitative analysis on preservation of general VLM conversational ability (Fig. 4, 5) is an interesting and practically relevant side-benefit that ties into the broader narrative about catastrophic forgetting in VLA fine-tuning.
weaknesses: There is a significant internal inconsistency: BayesianVLA's reported average success rate on SimplerEnv differs between Table 1 (66.5%, per-task 89.6/63.8/33.3/79.2) and Table 3 (63.5%, per-task 81.9/66.6/34.7/70.8) for what appears to be the identical method/backbone/benchmark. This discrepancy is never explained and casts doubt on the reliability and reproducibility of the reported numbers.

The abstract and introduction claim 'extensive experiments... on SimplerEnv and RoboCasa' and Section 4 states evaluation on 'four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2,' but only SimplerEnv and RoboCasa results are actually presented; LIBERO and RoboTwin2 results are absent and explicitly deferred to future work in the Limitations section. This mismatch between claimed and delivered scope suggests the paper was submitted in an unfinished state.

The description of the LLR loss (Eq. 7) and its implementation is underspecified: the text mentions computing a baseline p(ℓ|v) either 'by detaching gradients or using a separate pass,' but the actual mechanism for obtaining this baseline (a full second forward pass without Q? architecture details?) is not clearly specified, harming reproducibility of the central technical contribution.

No statistical significance information (variance across seeds/runs, confidence intervals) is reported for the main results despite running hundreds of trials per task; single-run point estimates are used to claim state-of-the-art performance and precise percentage gains (e.g., '11.3% improvement').

A closely related contemporaneous work with an almost identical framing ('Seeing to act, prompting to specify: A Bayesian factorization of vision language action policy', Xu et al. 2025) is cited only in passing in the catastrophic-forgetting discussion, with no comparison or discussion of how BayesianVLA differs from or improves upon this prior Bayesian-factorization approach to VLA, which undermines the originality claims.

Ablation studies are limited to a single benchmark (SimplerEnv) and a coarse three-way comparison; there is no exploration of key hyperparameters (number of latent queries K, loss weights λ and β) that would clarify sensitivity and robustness of the proposed method.

The claim of 'preserved general capabilities' rests on two anecdotal single-example qualitative comparisons (Fig. 4, 5) rather than any standard multimodal benchmark (e.g., MMBench, MMMU), which is insufficient evidence for the fairly strong claim made in Section 4.3.

Baseline comparisons in Table 1 draw numbers from disparate papers that may use different training data, embodiments, and protocols, which is common practice but is not clearly caveated, making some 'SOTA' claims less rigorous than a fully controlled comparison would allow.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and well-motivated pathology (the 'vision shortcut'/information collapse) in VLA training on goal-driven datasets, and supports it with several illustrative pilot experiments (RoboCasa, LIBERO Goal, Bridge->SimplerEnv) that are intuitive and informative.

The Bayesian decomposition framing (prior p(a|v) vs posterior π(a|v,ℓ)) gives a clean conceptual lens for a real failure mode, and the Latent Action Query bottleneck is an efficient architectural mechanism that is reused for both branches without extra inference-time cost.

Reported numbers show consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements over a matched baseline (QwenGR00T) on SimplerEnv and RoboCasa, and the ablation separates architectural (query) gains from the Bayesian/LLR objective gains.
The qualitative examples on preserved text/VLM capability are an interesting side observation connecting catastrophic forgetting to the vision-shortcut phenomenon.
weaknesses: Core objective (Eq. 7) is underspecified/ambiguous: the text says the 'baseline' log p(ℓ|v) can be obtained 'by detaching gradients or using a separate pass,' but the actual loss in Eq. 7 subtracts sg(log p(ℓ|v)) without clarifying which branch or computation actually produces this term, making the central training signal not reproducible from the paper alone.

The theoretical derivation treats a as a literal sampled action, but in practice the method substitutes the hidden state of learnable latent queries H_Q for a in p(ℓ|a,v); this substitution is a meaningful departure from the clean derivation in Appendix A and is not justified or discussed as an approximation.

The PMI/LLR estimator is a simple single-pair log-ratio without any contrastive/negative-sample structure, which is unusual and potentially biased/unstable as a PMI estimator; no analysis of its properties, bias, or sensitivity to β is provided.

Despite stating in the introduction that the paper evaluates on 'four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2,' only SimplerEnv and RoboCasa results are actually reported; LIBERO and RoboTwin2 results plus real-world experiments are explicitly deferred to 'future work'/'currently underway,' meaning the claimed experimental scope is not matched by the delivered evidence.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for any success-rate numbers despite stochastic simulation evaluation (480 trials aggregated into single point estimates for SimplerEnv, 50 trials for RoboCasa); 'state-of-the-art' claims are made without statistical testing, and RoboCasa per-task results are mixed (several tasks regress relative to baseline), which is not discussed critically.

Table 1 and Table 3 report different average success numbers for BayesianVLA on the same SimplerEnv benchmark (66.5% vs 63.5%) without explanation, undermining confidence in the reported results and reproducibility.

The qualitative evidence for 'preservation of general capabilities' (Section 4.3) rests on two anecdotal single-prompt examples rather than any standard VLM benchmark (e.g., MMMU, MathVista, general QA suites), which is insufficient support for the claim that BayesianVLA meaningfully preserves general reasoning/language ability.

A directly relevant prior work performing a similar Bayesian factorization of VLA policies (Xu et al., 2025, 'Seeing to act, prompting to specify: A Bayesian factorization of vision language action policy') is only cited in passing and not discussed or compared against in the related work section, leaving the novelty of the core Bayesian decomposition contribution unclear relative to concurrent work.
Key hyperparameters (λ, β, K=64 choice) are not reported with concrete values used in the main experiments nor accompanied by sensitivity analysis, limiting reproducibility.

The motivational experiments in Section 2 rely on a single base architecture (Qwen3VL-4B-GR00T via starVLA), yet the paper generalizes the 'vision shortcut' claim to 'current VLA models' broadly, which is a broader claim than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper provides a compelling and well-designed set of pilot experiments (RoboCasa, LIBERO, BridgeDataV2→SimplerEnv) that convincingly motivate the 'vision shortcut' / information collapse phenomenon, including a nice contrast between in-distribution success and OOD/ambiguous-task failure.

The Bayesian decomposition framing (prior p(a|v), posterior π(a|v,ℓ), PMI/LLR objective) is conceptually clean and gives a principled motivation for the proposed training signal, with a clear derivation in the appendix.

The Latent Action Query mechanism is an elegant architectural choice: by controlling token position under causal masking, the same VLM weights can realize both the prior and posterior branches without extra inference cost, and the ablation isolates its standalone benefit from the full Bayesian objective.

Reasonably broad empirical validation on two benchmarks (SimplerEnv, RoboCasa) with many strong recent baselines, showing consistent and sometimes large improvements (e.g., 11.3% average gain on SimplerEnv over the same-codebase baseline).

An interesting and underexplored side-benefit is identified and qualitatively demonstrated: the method appears to mitigate catastrophic forgetting of general language ability compared to the baseline, which is a relevant practical consideration for VLA post-training.
The ablation study clearly separates the contribution of the architectural change (action queries) from the proposed training objective (LLR), lending some support to the central claim.
weaknesses: The implementation of the LLR loss (Eq. 7) is under-specified and arguably inconsistent with its own derivation: the text says a baseline p(ℓ|v) should be computed 'by detaching gradients or using a separate pass,' but Eq. 7 provides no explicit mechanism for how this second term is computed in practice, leaving a key part of the method unreproducible from the text alone.

The approximation p(ℓ|a,v) ≈ p(ℓ|v, H_Q^prior) conflates a continuous hidden representation used to predict actions via flow matching with the actual ground-truth/generated action a referenced in the Bayesian derivation; this substitution is not theoretically justified and could be a loose approximation that weakens the claimed correspondence between the training loss and the PMI objective.

Section 4 states that experiments were conducted on 'four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2,' but only SimplerEnv and RoboCasa results are reported for BayesianVLA; LIBERO is used only in motivating pilot experiments (without the proposed method) and RoboTwin2 results are entirely absent, which is an overclaim relative to what is actually delivered in the paper.

There is an unexplained numerical discrepancy between the main SimplerEnv result (66.5% average, Table 1) and the ablation table's 'full BayesianVLA' result (63.5%, Table 3) under ostensibly the same backbone and setup, which raises reproducibility/consistency concerns.

No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported despite stochastic simulation evaluation (480 trials for SimplerEnv, 50 for RoboCasa), making it hard to assess whether reported gains (sometimes a few points) are statistically meaningful.

The paper explicitly states that broader benchmarks and real-world robot experiments are 'currently underway' and promises LIBERO/RoboTwin results and larger backbones 'in subsequent versions,' signaling the work is an interim/incomplete submission rather than a fully validated contribution.

Only a single backbone (Qwen3-VL-4B via StarVLA/QwenGR00T) and a single underlying codebase are used; generalization of the proposed Bayesian decomposition to other VLA architectures (e.g., π0.5, OpenVLA-OFT style backbones) is not empirically tested.

The qualitative language-preservation claims (Figures 4-5) are based on only one or two anecdotal examples rather than a systematic benchmark (e.g., standard LLM/VLM evaluation suites), limiting the strength of this secondary claim.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-designed empirical diagnosis of the 'vision shortcut' phenomenon through three complementary pilot experiments (ID testing, ambiguous LIBERO-Goal scenarios, and OOD SimplerEnv generalization), each isolating a different facet of the failure mode and collectively making a convincing case that goal-driven data collection induces near-vanishing conditional mutual information between instructions and actions.

The Bayesian/PMI formulation is theoretically motivated and cleanly derived (Appendix A), connecting the diagnosed pathology directly to a concrete training objective (LLR maximization) rather than just describing the problem qualitatively.

The Latent Action Query architecture is a neat and practically appealing design: it uses causal masking to cheaply instantiate two conditioning regimes with shared weights, imposes an information bottleneck that decouples DiT complexity from VLM context length, and incurs zero additional inference-time cost, which is empirically substantiated.

Evaluation is broad (SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, LIBERO, two independent real-world manipulation setups with blocks and vegetables) and the gains are consistently larger precisely in the ambiguous/OOD conditions the paper's own theory predicts should benefit most (e.g., LIBERO-Goal, SimplerEnv OOD tasks, unseen-color real-world block), which is a meaningful internal consistency check rather than only aggregate improvement.

The ablations are thorough and go beyond simple component removal: they include hyperparameter sweeps (λ, β), query-count sensitivity, and, notably, a well-designed control experiment (auxiliary p(ℓ|v) loss) that helps distinguish 'generic language preservation' from 'action-relevant language grounding,' strengthening the causal story behind the LLR objective.

The qualitative analysis of catastrophic forgetting preservation (Figures 4-6) is a useful side contribution showing the proposed objective has beneficial side effects on retaining general VLM capabilities, an issue of practical relevance to the VLA community.
weaknesses: There are internal numerical inconsistencies that undermine confidence in reported results: the abstract claims an '11.3%' OOD SimplerEnv improvement while the introduction claims '8.8%' improvement for what appears to be the same comparison, and Section 4.5 refers to 'the full LangForce (63.5%)' when Table 5 reports 66.5%, suggesting insufficient proofreading of key quantitative claims.

The practical instantiation of the LLR objective (Eq. 7) is only loosely justified relative to the theoretical PMI decomposition (Eq. 4/12): the paper uses VLM language-modeling loss as a 'proxy' for p(ℓ|a,v) and p(ℓ|v), but the exact correspondence between the causal-masking trick and the target quantities is explained informally in prose rather than rigorously, leaving room for doubt about whether the optimized quantity faithfully approximates PMI or merely encourages some correlated but distinct behavior.

The most directly comparable prior work, BayesVLA (Xu et al., 2025), which also performs a Bayesian decomposition for VLA instruction following, is discussed only qualitatively in related work and is never empirically compared against LangForce in any table, which is a notable gap given how central this comparison would be to establishing the paper's incremental contribution (single-stage vs. two-stage training).

Most reported baseline numbers are taken from original papers rather than reproduced under identical settings; while the authors attempt to control for training data overlap, differences in backbones, compute budgets, and evaluation protocols across papers make some head-to-head comparisons (e.g., against π0.5, Isaac-GR00T-N1.6) less rigorous than a fully controlled ablation would be.

Real-world evaluations use small sample sizes (30 trials per condition) and, for the more interesting OOD conditions, absolute success rates remain low for all methods (e.g., 9/30 and 3/30 for LangForce), which limits the strength of claims about practical OOD generalization despite relative improvements over baselines.

Gains are not uniformly positive across all sub-tasks/settings (e.g., some RoboCasa 'PnP Novel' subsets and some SimplerEnv tasks show baselines or competitors outperforming LangForce), and no statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided for the many success-rate comparisons, making it hard to assess whether some reported differences are meaningful.

strengths: The paper provides a well-motivated empirical case for the 'vision shortcut'/information collapse phenomenon through three complementary pilot studies (ID RoboCasa, ambiguous LIBERO-Goal, OOD SimplerEnv), which together make a reasonably convincing qualitative argument that goal-driven VLA datasets encourage policies to ignore language.

The proposed Latent Action Query + dual-branch architecture is a practical, lightweight way to instantiate a vision-only prior and a vision+language posterior within a single shared VLM, and the method adds no inference-time overhead, which is a genuine engineering advantage over prior two-stage Bayesian approaches (e.g., BayesVLA).

Evaluation breadth is reasonably large: SimplerEnv, RoboCasa (24 tasks), LIBERO, and two real-robot settings (colored blocks and vegetables), along with ablations on query count, λ, β, and an auxiliary language-prediction control, which helps probe several aspects of the method.

The qualitative demonstration that LangForce better preserves text-only conversational ability relative to the QwenGR00T baseline is an interesting side-finding connecting the Bayesian objective to mitigation of catastrophic forgetting of language ability.
weaknesses: There are unresolved numerical inconsistencies that undermine trust in the reported results: the abstract states an '11.3% improvement on OOD SimplerEnv' while the introduction's contribution list states '8.8% improvement in OOD generalization on SimplerEnv' for the same claim; similarly, Section 4.5 states the full LangForce achieves '63.5%' on SimplerEnv while Table 5 reports 66.5% for the same row. These discrepancies are not minor typos in isolation but recur across central claims, raising concern about the care taken in reporting results.

The derivation linking the theoretical PMI objective (Eq. 4, which involves p(ℓ|a,v) conditioned on an actual action a) to the practical LLR loss (Eq. 7) is not rigorous: Eq. 7 conditions the language-modeling probability on the Priori Branch's hidden state H^prior_Q, which is only a pre-action representation produced before the diffusion action head, not the sampled/generated action itself. The paper does not justify why this hidden-state-level proxy faithfully captures p(ℓ|a,v) rather than simply p(ℓ|v) with an alternative context ordering, leaving the core theoretical contribution only loosely connected to its implementation.

The architectural (Latent Action Query) and objective (LLR) contributions are entangled in the ablations; Table 5 only isolates '+Action Query' vs. full LangForce, but there is no ablation of the dual-branch flow-matching objective alone (λ>0, β=0, without architectural changes beyond baseline) that would cleanly separate the benefit of the proposed Bayesian objective from the benefit of the query-bottleneck architecture across all experiments, beyond the SimplerEnv table.

Comparisons against external baselines (π0, π0.5, Isaac-GR00T, OpenVLA-OFT, etc. in Table 1) mix different base VLM architectures, model sizes, and training data recipes, with success metrics taken from original papers rather than reproduced under identical settings; while the paper controls for this to some extent by comparing primarily to its own QwenGR00T baseline, the 'state-of-the-art' framing against heterogeneous baselines is not fully substantiated.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for success rates despite using finite trial counts (480 or 50 trials), making it difficult to judge whether several reported gains (e.g., 0.3–2% differences in LIBERO suites or ablation hyperparameter sweeps) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The conceptual contribution overlaps substantially with the cited BayesVLA (Xu et al., 2025), which also performs a Bayesian decomposition of vision-only prior and language posterior; the paper's primary differentiation (single-stage vs. two-stage training) is a meaningful but incremental advance rather than a fundamentally new idea, and the paper does not include a direct empirical comparison against BayesVLA on a shared benchmark.

The Impact Statement is generic boilerplate ('none which we feel must be specifically highlighted') despite the paper concerning physical robot manipulation policies, where failure modes (e.g., confidently executing the wrong physical action due to residual vision shortcuts) could have safety implications worth discussing.

strengths: The paper provides a well-designed suite of pilot experiments (Section 2) across three distinct settings (in-distribution testing, ambiguous multi-task scenes in LIBERO-Goal, and OOD generalization from BridgeDataV2/Fractal to SimplerEnv) that convincingly illustrate the 'vision shortcut' phenomenon with concrete success-rate and loss-curve evidence, rather than relying on the hypothesis alone.

The proposed Bayesian/PMI-based formulation (Eq. 1-4, derived in Appendix A) is conceptually clean and connects naturally to an efficient architectural instantiation (Latent Action Queries with causal masking) that requires no extra inference cost, which is a practically valuable design choice.

Experimental coverage is broad: three simulation benchmarks (SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, LIBERO) plus two real-world manipulation settings (colored blocks and vegetables) with OOD generalization tests, and consistent improvement over the matched baseline (QwenGR00T) across all of them.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of the architecture (Latent Action Queries alone) versus the dual-branch Bayesian/LLR objective, and further ablate λ, β, and the number of queries, strengthening the causal claim that the LLR objective (not just the architecture) drives the gains.

An interesting secondary finding is that the LLR objective appears to mitigate catastrophic forgetting of general language ability, supported by qualitative examples and a sensible control ablation (auxiliary p(ℓ|v) loss) showing the effect is not merely due to retaining an auxiliary language loss.
weaknesses: The core idea overlaps substantially with the concurrent/prior work BayesVLA (Xu et al., 2025), which also performs Bayesian decomposition of vision and language-conditioned policies; the paper's main differentiator (single-stage vs. two-stage training) is a relatively narrow technical distinction, which somewhat limits the claimed originality.

The practical instantiation of the LLR objective treats the VLM's language-modeling loss on instruction tokens as a direct proxy for log p(ℓ|a,v) and log p(ℓ|v), but this connection is not rigorously justified—particularly since the 'action' information is only implicitly encoded through hidden states feeding back into language prediction, and no empirical verification (e.g., does the LLR term actually track a sensible estimate of PMI during training) is provided beyond the NLL/PPL analysis on a single LIBERO-Goal subset.

Cross-architecture baseline comparisons (Table 1) mix models with different VLM backbones, parameter counts, and training data scales (e.g., π0, π0.5, CogACT), making the headline SOTA claims less interpretable than the controlled QwenGR00T-vs-LangForce comparison, which is the only truly apples-to-apples result.

There is an internal inconsistency in the text: Section 4.5 states 'full LangForce (63.5%)' while Table 5 reports LangForce's average as 66.5%, suggesting insufficient proofreading of quantitative claims.

Statistical robustness is not fully addressed—no variance/seed information is given for the simulation results (single run per configuration implied), and real-world trials (30 per condition) are modest in scale for drawing strong conclusions about OOD generalization differences (e.g., 9/30 vs 2/30).
The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential considerations around deploying language-conditioned manipulation policies in real-world settings.

The claim that 'ambiguous data collection' is the long-term fix (Section 6) is stated somewhat speculatively without supporting evidence beyond the LIBERO-Goal case, and the broader applicability of the 'Information Collapse' diagnosis to the large-scale OXE/Fractal/BridgeV2 training data used in the main SimplerEnv experiments is not directly measured (only inferred from loss curves).
